content: 1. Isoniazid-monoresistant tuberculosis (TB) and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) require specific treatment regimens, and the effectiveness of daily versus intermittent administration should be evaluated. 2. Adolescents should be included in clinical trials to better understand the efficacy and safety of TB treatments in this population. 3. Children should be included in Phase 4 trials of new TB drugs to assess long-term safety and effectiveness. 4. The prevention of TB in children includes the use of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination. The risk of BCG-related disease in HIV-positive infants receiving early antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be determined. 5. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate the incidence and management of BCG-immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (BCG-IRIS). 6. Effective preventive therapy strategies for child contacts of drug-resistant TB cases should be developed and evaluated. 7. Symptom-based screening tools for identifying TB in child contacts, including those who are HIV-positive or HIV-negative, should be assessed for their effectiveness. 8. The safety, efficacy, and optimal duration of novel preventive therapy regimens in children should be evaluated, including cost-benefit analyses. 9. Operational challenges in the contact-tracing process for implementing wide-scale isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) should be identified and addressed. 10. Strategies to enhance adherence to preventive therapy in children should be developed. 11. The risk of developing drug-resistant TB among children receiving preventive therapy should be determined. 12. The length of treatment time required before a child with drug-susceptible or drug-resistant TB can return to school without posing a transmission risk should be clarified. 13. The use of routinely collected data to optimize TB treatment outcomes in children should be improved. 14. Reporting and management of childhood TB contacts should be standardized. 15. Barriers to reporting TB cases in children, including those encountered in the private healthcare sector, should be identified and addressed. 16. National tuberculosis programs should provide guidance on the management of TB in children, including the reporting of drug-resistant TB cases and treatment outcomes, as well as adverse effects of treatment. 17. Indicators for assessing the quality of care in TB management should be developed. 18. Barriers to accessing healthcare and integrated services for TB should be investigated. 19. Models for integrated care, particularly for maternal and infant TB care, should be developed and evaluated. 20. Access to integrated support for families affected by TB should be assessed. 21. Models for integrating nutritional support into TB and HIV programs should be developed and evaluated. 22. The cost-effectiveness of integrated nutritional support in TB and HIV programs should be investigated. 23. The Xpert MTB/RIF system, which uses automated real-time nucleic acid amplification technology, should be used as the initial diagnostic test for children suspected of having MDR-TB or HIV-associated TB, rather than conventional microscopy and culture. 24. Xpert MTB/RIF may also be used as the initial test for all children suspected of having TB, acknowledging resource implications. 25. For children suspected of having extrapulmonary TB, Xpert MTB/RIF may replace conventional methods (e.g., microscopy, culture, histopathology) for testing specific non-respiratory specimens, such as lymph nodes and other tissues. 26. Xpert MTB/RIF should be used preferentially for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimens in children suspected of having TB meningitis, given the urgency of rapid diagnosis. 27. Children with a single negative Xpert MTB/RIF result should undergo further diagnostic testing, and those with high clinical suspicion for TB should be treated even if the test result is negative or unavailable. 28. Pleural fluid is a suboptimal sample for bacterial confirmation of pleural TB using any method, and pleural biopsy is preferred. However, a positive Xpert MTB/RIF result from pleural fluid should prompt treatment for pleural TB, while negative results should be followed by additional tests. 29. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) should not replace the tuberculin skin test (TST) in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing latent TB infection in children or for the diagnostic work-up of children suspected of TB disease, regardless of HIV status. 30. IGRAs and TST have similar accuracy in detecting TB infection and disease in children, but IGRAs are expensive, technically challenging, and require sophisticated laboratory support. Indeterminate results are common, especially in young children. 31. A negative IGRA, like a negative TST, cannot exclude TB disease.
